title: Descending Factorial Identity: C(n,k)·k! = n·(n-1)·⋯·(n-k+1)
description: Formalizes the descending (falling) factorial analogue of the arithmetic series identity. Proves C(n,k)·k! = n.descFactorial(k) — the ordered selection formula counting k-permutations of n objects.

meta.author: Lean Genius

overview.historicalContext:
The binomial coefficient C(n,k) counts unordered k-element subsets of an n-element set. Multiplying by k! gives the number of ordered selections (k-permutations): C(n,k)·k! = n·(n-1)·⋯·(n-k+1) = n.descFactorial(k). This identity appears throughout combinatorics, probability, and algebra.

The parent file (ArithmeticSeriesOQ02OQ04) proved the ascending (rising) factorial analogue: C(n+k,k)·k! = (n+1)·(n+2)·⋯·(n+k) = ascFactorial(n+1, k). This file proves the complementary descending case and establishes the duality between the two forms.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that C(n,k)·k! = n.descFactorial(k) = n·(n-1)·⋯·(n-k+1), the descending factorial identity for binomial coefficients.
overview.proofStrategy: The main identity follows directly from Mathlib's `Nat.descFactorial_eq_factorial_mul_choose`. The product formula unfolds via `Nat.descFactorial_eq_prod_range`. Structural properties (full factorial identity, divisibility, self-case) follow from Mathlib lemmas. Low-dimensional cases are verified by `simp` + `ring`.
keyInsights: Descending: C(n,k)*k! = n*(n-1)*...*(n-k+1) counts ordered k-selections from {1,...,n}
Ascending: C(n+k,k)*k! = (n+1)*...*(n+k) counts ordered k-selections with offset n
These are dual: same count, different parameterization of the starting point
The Mathlib key: Nat.descFactorial_eq_factorial_mul_choose gives the main result directly
descFactorial(n, n) = n! recovers the full factorial as a special case

conclusion.summary: Proved the descending factorial identity C(n,k)·k! = n.descFactorial(k) and 10 consequences. 169 lines, 11 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Dual to the ascending factorial identity in ArithmeticSeriesOQ02OQ04.
conclusion.implications: Together with the ascending factorial result, this completes the symmetry between rising and falling factorials in the context of arithmetic series and binomial coefficients. Both forms are useful in combinatorics: the descending form appears in falling factorial polynomials (basis for umbral calculus) and the ascending form in rising factorial polynomials (Pochhammer symbols).
